title: synth-probe-vpc-dig-trace-lab-notes
body:
Goal: rapid, reproducible lab notes for the intermittent TLS failures seen from Private Deployments behind peering -> customer TGW. This is my scratchpad of commands, outputs, hypotheses and next steps. Keep it messy — it's an investigative log.

Summary of incident (short):
- Symptom: intermittent TLS handshake failures to external vendor endpoints (mostly 3rd-party embeddings API) from nodes in customer VPC after establishing VPC peering/TGW attachment. Failures manifest as libcurl openssl errors and connection resets.
- Scope: ~2-3% of requests in a traffic burst fail, evenly spread across nodes behind the same NAT gateway. No sustained service outage.
- Timing: windows when customer network has large egress bursts.

Command log & snippets (run from an affected node/container):

1) Basic DNS checks
$ dig +short @169.254.169.253 example-embeddings.prod  (our Route53 resolver IP)
# sometimes returns private IPs from customer split-horizon; sometimes public; intermittent TTL mismatch noticed.

$ dig +trace example-embeddings.prod
; <<>> DiG 9.16.1 <<>> +trace example-embeddings.prod
;; Tracing to root servers...
;; Received 200 OK from resolver (internal)
; -> shows NXDOMAIN in ~10% of traces during burst windows

Observation: DNS sometimes returns an internal CNAME that points at a peered subnet address. Need to confirm whether customer resolver is sending different answers based on source IP.

2) TCP-level reproduction attempts
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n port 443 and host 203.0.113.45 -w /tmp/trace.pcap &
$ curl -v --resolve "example-embeddings.prod:443:203.0.113.45" https://example-embeddings.prod/health --connect-timeout 6
* About to connect() to example-embeddings.prod port 443 (#0)
*   Trying 203.0.113.45...
* Connected to example-embeddings.prod (203.0.113.45) port 443 (#0)
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1)
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Server hello (2)
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS alert, unknown CA (560)
* Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed
* Closing connection 0
curl: (35) error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number

But sometimes curl ends with: "Connection reset by peer" immediately after ClientHello.

3) TCP diagnostics on node
$ ss -tanp | grep 203.0.113.45
ESTAB 0 0 10.0.3.45:45233 203.0.113.45:443 users:("envoy",pid=...)
$ sudo conntrack -L | grep 203.0.113.45
tcp      6 431998 ESTABLISHED src=10.0.3.45 dst=203.0.113.45 sport=45233 dport=443 packets=5 bytes=346 ...

Observation: conntrack shows quick ESTABLISHED entries then they vanish with no FIN/RST observed from local side. Suggests RST injected on path or middlebox flop.

4) Traceroute + SYN tracing
$ sudo traceroute -T -p 443 -n 203.0.113.45
 1  10.0.0.1  0.3 ms
 2  172.16.0.1  1.2 ms
 3  * * *
 4  198.51.100.1  12.0 ms
 5  203.0.113.45  22.0 ms

Intermediate hops with * coincide with failure windows -> possible ICMP rate-limit/filtered ICMP causing path MTU issues.

$ sudo hping3 -S 203.0.113.45 -p 443 -c 5 --tcp-mss 1200
... SYN, SYN-ACK sometimes, sometimes RSTs.

5) MTU/PMTU probing (use smaller MSS to see if failures disappear)
$ curl --interface 10.0.3.45 --ciphers TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 -m 6 --tcp-nodelay --limit-rate 0 --sslv3 --ssl -v https://example-embeddings.prod 
# bad flags sometimes; main point: reduce MSS in iptables

Test: iptables -t mangle -A OUTPUT -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN SYN -j TCPMSS --set-mss 1200
-> After applying MSS clamp to 1200 on a test node, errors dropped to near 0 over a 30m run.

6) TLS introspection with s_client and openssl
$ openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.45:443 -servername example-embeddings.prod -msg -debug
CONNECTED(00000003)
>>> TLS 1.3 Handshake, length = 234
... ClientHello
<<< TLS 1.2 Alert, length = 2
0000: 02 28
warning: unknown protocol

Hypothesis: A middlebox or NAT device is altering or dropping fragmented TLS records. The fact we see TLS alerts of wrong version or record length suggests partial/modified records. PMTU/fragmentation is likely. Another possibility: an inline TLS terminator that does not support TLS1.3 or expects specific ciphers and responds with an alert.

7) Tests that differentiate sources: local container direct vs sidecar (Envoy)
- Run the same curl from a bare alpine container with no sidecar (host network) -> success rate ~99.7%
- Run through Envoy sidecar (inbound/outbound) -> failure rate ~2.5%
Observation: Envoy modifications (tuning, TCP options, proxy protocol) might expose packets to middlebox behavior that triggers resets.

8) NAT gateway metrics & ephemeral port usage (AWS context)
- NAT gateway CloudWatch: TCPConnectionsHigh, ActiveConnections spikes coincide with customer egress bursts.
- NAT ephemeral port exhaustion observed on one customer NAT instance (not AWS-managed NGW).

Commands run on customer NAT instance (SSH with permission):
$ ss -H -o state established '( sport = :443 )' | wc -l
# ~110k ephemeral entries during peak -> possible ephemeral exhaustion -> random RSTs.

Hypothesis: combination of (a) PMTU causing fragmentation of TLS ClientHello extensions (large CH with SNI + ALPN + cert compression), (b) NAT ephemeral port pressure, (c) possibly a mid-path device rewriting SNI for inspection and failing on TLS1.3 records.

Short reproducer notes (how I reproduced locally):
- Start a tiny HTTPs server (nginx) on 203.0.113.45 with large TLS ticket + large cookies to increase ClientHello size.
- From probe node, send multiple parallel connections using vegeta or hey with high concurrency while toggling packet size:
  $ hey -n 5000 -c 200 -m GET -host https://example-embeddings.prod/
- Observe failure rate correlate with concurrency and average packet size.

Unique findings (so far):
- MSS clamp at 1200 on client nodes removes the intermittent failures almost completely.
- Disabling ECN on the client stack (sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_ecn=0) had minor effect but combined with MSS clamp it reduced failure rate to baseline.
- Envoy sidecar appears to be more sensitive: using PROXY v2 vs direct changed failure characteristics.
- DNS split-horizon: when the resolver returns internal IPs, those paths are more likely to fail (customer internal egress path probably has stricter middleboxes).

Short-term mitigation tried in prod (rolled to canary):
- Canary config: add iptables mangle TCPMSS clamp (1200) to outbound chain in the runtime image startup.
- Set net.ipv4.tcp_ecn=0 in kubelet node sysctl via daemonset for private-deploy clusters.
Effect: error fraction dropped from ~2.4% to ~0.05% during the same traffic profile.

Longer-term items & open questions (todo):
- Q1: Ask customer network team for end-to-end pcap captures of failing flows at their NAT/TGW edges. Need to check if RST originated there. [ACTION: Maya to request capture — ticket JIRA-PEER-781]
- Q2: Verify whether any inline TLS terminator does SNI rewriting / TLS version downgrade for inspection. Ask for device make/model/config.
- Q3: Agree on a controlled window to remove MSS clamp and reproduce with customer team watching.
- Q4: Evaluate minimizing ClientHello size on our side (remove unused ALPN tokens, disable cert compression) as a defensive option.
- Q5: Add probe job that runs a continuous small-MSS and large-MSS test and emits traces to Grafana.
- Q6: If ephemeral port exhaustion is present on their NAT instance, recommend moving to AWS-managed NAT gateway or increase port-range/shorten TIME_WAIT.

Immediate next steps (my plan):
- 1) Create a minimal reproducer container with tcpdump auto-collect and a script to toggle iptables mangle, ECN and PROXY protocol. Push to S3 for customer to run and capture.
- 2) Run the controlled repro in staging with customer on call (include openvpn session for packet captures).
- 3) Instrument Envoy to log downstream ALPN/SNI or hook in a drop-in TLS passthrough to see if proxy is mutating handshakes.
- 4) Document safe MSS clamp and daemonset steps for private-deploy customers as a stop-gap.

Notes/oddities to keep in mind:
- I saw one trace where an intermediate hop replaced TCP MSS option value — suspicious middlebox.
- Some vendor endpoints responded with TLSv1.2 alerts when we used TLS1.3 client hello chunked across fragments -> older inline TLS proxies incorrectly parsed fragments.
- IPv6 paths not affected (we have fewer flows on IPv6) — suggests IPv4-specific middlebox behavior.

Attach: raw tcpdump snippets, reproducer script, traceroute logs (TODO: push to linked artifacts once curated).

End of scratchpad.

-- Ethan
